\chapter{Chapter02 — Boolean Influence}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from FABL.Chapter02.InfluencesAndDerivatives.BooleanInfluence
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter02.InfluencesAndDerivatives.BooleanInfluence}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Coordinate replacement]
\lean{FABL.setCoordinate}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.setCoordinate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
Let $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, choose a coordinate $i$, and choose a sign $b\in\{-1,1\}$. The
coordinate replacement of $x$ is the Boolean-cube point that has value $b$ at coordinate
$i$ and agrees with $x$ at every other coordinate.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Value at the updated coordinate]
\lean{FABL.setCoordinate_apply_self}
\label{FABL.setCoordinate_apply_self}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $x$ be a sign vector on $n$ coordinates, and let $i$ be
a coordinate. Replacing the value at coordinate $i$ by a sign $b$ makes the value at
that coordinate equal to $b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Effect of changing a coordinate]
\lean{FABL.setCoordinate_apply_of_ne}
\label{FABL.setCoordinate_apply_of_ne}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $x$ be a vector of signs indexed by the coordinates in
$\text{Fin }n$, and let $i,j \,\in\, \text{Fin }n$ satisfy $j \ne i$. Replacing the value
of $x$ at coordinate $i$ by any sign $b$ leaves its value at coordinate $j$ unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Updating a coordinate by its existing value]
\lean{FABL.setCoordinate_eq_self}
\label{FABL.setCoordinate_eq_self}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{1}
For any natural number $n$, sign vector $x\in\{−1,1\}^{n}$, and coordinate
$i\in\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, replacing the value of $x$ at $i$ by $x_i$ leaves $x$ unchanged.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Successive updates at one coordinate]
\lean{FABL.setCoordinate_setCoordinate}
\label{FABL.setCoordinate_setCoordinate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $x$ be a sign vector on $n$ coordinates, and let $i$ be
a coordinate. Replacing coordinate $i$ first by $a$ and then by $b$ has the same effect
as replacing it directly by $b$, for any signs $a$ and $b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Coordinate flip]
\lean{FABL.flipCoordinate}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p018-b007}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.flipCoordinate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.setCoordinate}
For a nonnegative integer $n$, a sign vector $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, and a coordinate
$i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, the coordinate flip of $x$ at $i$ is the sign vector obtained by
replacing its $i$th entry with its negative and leaving all other entries unchanged.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Flipping a coordinate twice]
\lean{FABL.flipCoordinate_flipCoordinate}
\label{FABL.flipCoordinate_flipCoordinate}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate_apply_self}
\difficulty{3}
For every sign vector $x\in\{−1,1\}^n$ and coordinate $i$, flipping coordinate $i$ twice
returns $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Pivotal coordinate]
\lean{FABL.IsPivotal}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p223-b003
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.IsPivotal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.flipCoordinate}
For a function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\beta$, a coordinate $i$, and a sign vector $x$, the
coordinate $i$ is pivotal for $f$ at $x$ if $f(x)$ differs from the value of $f$ at the
vector obtained by flipping coordinate $i$ of $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pivotality via the two coordinate values]
\lean{FABL.isPivotal_iff_setCoordinate_ne}
\label{FABL.isPivotal_iff_setCoordinate_ne}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsPivotal, FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate_eq_self}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\beta$ be any function, let $i$ be a
coordinate, and let $x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. The function is pivotal at $x$ in coordinate $i$
if and only if its values at the two inputs obtained from $x$ by setting coordinate $i$
to $+1$ and to $-1$ are different.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Boolean influence]
\lean{FABL.booleanInfluence}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p213-b005
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p007-b003}
\label{FABL.booleanInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.IsPivotal, FABL.uniformProbability}
Let $f$ be a Boolean function on the sign cube of dimension $n$, taking values in
$\{\pm1\}$. The influence of coordinate $i$ is the uniform probability, over sign
vectors $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, that flipping coordinate $i$ changes the value of $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coordinate face of the sign cube]
\lean{FABL.DimensionEdge}
\label{FABL.DimensionEdge}
\leanok
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $i$ be one of its coordinates. The dimension
edge at $i$ is the set of sign vectors in ${-1,1}^n$ whose $i$th coordinate equals $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sign and coordinate face parametrization]
\lean{FABL.signProdDimensionEdgeEquiv}
\label{FABL.signProdDimensionEdgeEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge, FABL.Sign, FABL.setCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate_apply_self, FABL.setCoordinate_eq_self, FABL.setCoordinate_setCoordinate}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $i$ be one of its coordinates. Every sign
vector in ${-1,1}^n$ is uniquely specified by its sign at coordinate $i$ together with
a sign vector whose $i$th coordinate is $1$; equivalently, the product of the two
element sign set and the dimension edge at $i$ is in bijection with ${-1,1}^n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Cardinality of a sign-cube face]
\lean{FABL.card_dimensionEdge}
\label{FABL.card_dimensionEdge}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge, FABL.Sign, FABL.SignCube, FABL.signProdDimensionEdgeEquiv}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $i$ be a coordinate with $0\\le i<n$. Among the sign
vectors in $\\{-1,1\\}^n$, the vectors whose $i$th coordinate is $1$ form a set of
cardinality $2^{n-1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Probability of a singleton]
\lean{FABL.uniformProbability_eq_singleton}
\label{FABL.uniformProbability_eq_singleton}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformProbability}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\\Omega$ be a finite nonempty set and let $a\\in\\Omega$. The uniform probability
of the event consisting only of $a$ is $1/|\\Omega|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Boundary edge]
\lean{FABL.IsBoundaryDimensionEdge}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b004}
\label{FABL.IsBoundaryDimensionEdge}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.DimensionEdge, FABL.flipCoordinate}
Let $f$ be a Boolean function on the sign cube of dimension $n$, taking values in
$\{\pm1\}$, and let $i$ be a coordinate. A dimension edge at $i$ is a sign vector $x$
with $x_i=1$. Such an edge is a boundary edge for $f$ if $f(x)$ differs from its value
at the vector obtained by flipping coordinate $i$ of $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dimension edge boundary fraction]
\lean{FABL.dimensionEdgeBoundaryFraction}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b004}
\label{FABL.dimensionEdgeBoundaryFraction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.IsBoundaryDimensionEdge, FABL.uniformProbability}
Let $f$ be a Boolean function on the sign cube of dimension $n$, taking values in
$\{\pm1\}$, and let $i$ be a coordinate. The dimension edge boundary fraction at $i$ is
the uniform probability, among sign vectors $x$ with $x_i=1$, that flipping coordinate
$i$ changes the value of $f$.
\end{definition}

For either sign $\sigma\in\{\pm1\}$, form $x$ by replacing coordinate $i$ of $e$ with
$\sigma$. For any Boolean function $f$, $f$ is pivotal at $x$ in coordinate $i$ if and
only if $f(e)$ differs from its value at the input obtained by flipping coordinate $i$
of $e$.
\end{theorem}

coordinate. The influence of $f$ in coordinate $i$ equals the fraction of points on the
face where coordinate $i$ is $+1$ for which flipping coordinate $i$ changes the value of
$f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Pivotality of a dictator]
\lean{FABL.isPivotal_dictator_iff}
\label{FABL.isPivotal_dictator_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsPivotal, FABL.dictator, FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $i,j$ be coordinates in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let
$x\in\{\pm1\}^n$. The dictator that returns the value of coordinate $i$ is pivotal at
$x$ in coordinate $j$ if and only if $j=i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Pivotality under sign negation]
\lean{FABL.isPivotal_neg_iff}
\label{FABL.isPivotal_neg_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.IsPivotal}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$, and let $i$ be a coordinate and $x$
an input. The function $-f$, obtained by negating every output of $f$, is pivotal at $x$
in coordinate $i$ if and only if $f$ is pivotal there.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Negation preserves influence]
\lean{FABL.booleanInfluence_neg}
\label{FABL.booleanInfluence_neg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.booleanInfluence, FABL.isPivotal_neg_iff, FABL.uniformProbability}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ map the $n$-dimensional sign cube to $\\{−1,1\\}$,
and let $i$ be one of its coordinates. The probability that flipping coordinate $i$
changes the value of $f$ is unchanged when every output of $f$ is negated.
\end{theorem}

cube. For the function that outputs the negative of coordinate $i$, the influence of

\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
For any nonnegative integer $n$, any sign $c$, and any coordinate $i$ of the
$n$-dimensional sign cube, the constant function with value $c$ has influence zero in
coordinate $i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Constant positive point on a dimension edge]
\lean{FABL.allOneDimensionEdge}
\label{FABL.allOneDimensionEdge}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge}
For a positive integer $n$ and a coordinate $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the all-positive sign
vector belongs to the dimension edge where coordinate $i$ is fixed at $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Mostly negative point on a dimension edge]
\lean{FABL.allNegOneDimensionEdge}
\label{FABL.allNegOneDimensionEdge}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge}
For a positive integer $n$ and a coordinate $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the sign vector whose
$i$th coordinate is $1$ and whose other coordinates are all $-1$ belongs to the
dimension edge where coordinate $i$ is fixed at $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Boundary edges of the OR function]
\lean{FABL.isBoundaryDimensionEdge_orFunction_iff}
\label{FABL.isBoundaryDimensionEdge_orFunction_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge, FABL.IsBoundaryDimensionEdge, FABL.allOneDimensionEdge, FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.orFunction, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $i$ be a coordinate of the sign cube $\\{-1,1\\}^n$,
and let $e$ be an edge in direction $i$ whose endpoint has coordinate $i$ equal to $1$.
The OR function takes different values at the two endpoints of $e$ if and only if every
coordinate of its endpoint is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Boundary edges of the AND function]
\lean{FABL.isBoundaryDimensionEdge_andFunction_iff}
\label{FABL.isBoundaryDimensionEdge_andFunction_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge, FABL.IsBoundaryDimensionEdge, FABL.allNegOneDimensionEdge, FABL.andFunction, FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $i$ be a coordinate among the $n$ coordinates, and let
$e$ be a point of the cube whose $i$th coordinate is $1$. The AND function changes value
across the edge obtained by flipping coordinate $i$ at $e$ if and only if every
coordinate other than $i$ of $e$ is $-1$.
\end{theorem}

influence $1/2^{n-1}$ at coordinate $i$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
For a positive integer $n$ and a coordinate $i$ of the $n$-dimensional sign cube, the
influence of the function that equals $-1$ exactly when every input coordinate is $-1$
is $1/2^{n-1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Removing the fixed coordinate]
\lean{FABL.dimensionEdgeRemoveEquiv}
\label{FABL.dimensionEdgeRemoveEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge}
For a nonnegative integer $k$ and a coordinate $i$ among $k+1$ coordinates, the sign
vectors of length $k+1$ with coordinate $i$ fixed at $1$ are in bijection with sign
vectors of length $k$. The bijection deletes coordinate $i$, and its inverse inserts $1$
at coordinate $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sign vectors and coordinate subsets]
\lean{FABL.signCubeEquivFinset}
\label{FABL.signCubeEquivFinset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.positiveCoordinateSet}
For each nonnegative integer $k$, sign vectors of length $k$ are in bijection with
subsets of the $k$ coordinates: a sign vector corresponds to the set of coordinates
where its value is $1$, and a subset corresponds to the sign vector that is $1$ on that
subset and $-1$ elsewhere.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Cardinality of the positive-coordinate set]
\lean{FABL.signCubeEquivFinset_apply_card}
\label{FABL.signCubeEquivFinset_apply_card}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.positiveCoordinateCount, FABL.signCubeEquivFinset}
\difficulty{1}
For any $k\ge 0$ and sign vector $x\in\{−1,1\}^k$, the cardinality of the set of
coordinates where $x$ equals $1$ is the positive-coordinate count of $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Distribution of the positive-coordinate count]
\lean{FABL.uniformProbability_positiveCoordinateCount_eq}
\label{FABL.uniformProbability_positiveCoordinateCount_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.positiveCoordinateCount, FABL.signCubeEquivFinset, FABL.signCubeEquivFinset_apply_card, FABL.uniformProbability}
\difficulty{4}
For natural numbers $k$ and $r$, the uniform probability that a uniformly chosen point
of $\{−1,1\}^k$ has exactly $r$ coordinates equal to $1$ is $\binom{k}{r}/2^k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Boundary edges of odd-dimensional majority]
\lean{FABL.isBoundaryDimensionEdge_majority_odd_iff}
\label{FABL.isBoundaryDimensionEdge_majority_odd_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.DimensionEdge, FABL.IsBoundaryDimensionEdge, FABL.dimensionEdgeRemoveEquiv, FABL.flipCoordinate, FABL.majority, FABL.positiveCoordinateCount, FABL.setCoordinate, FABL.signValue, FABL.sum_signValue_eq_two_mul_positiveCoordinateCount_sub, FABL.thresholdSign, FABL.thresholdSign_of_neg, FABL.thresholdSign_of_nonneg}
\difficulty{5}
Let $m$ be a natural number, choose a coordinate $i$ among $2m+1$ coordinates, and let
$e$ be a cube point whose $i$th coordinate is $1$. The majority function on the
$(2m+1)$-dimensional cube changes value across the edge at $e$ in coordinate $i$ if and
only if, among the other $2m$ coordinates, exactly $m$ are equal to $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence of odd-dimensional majority]
\lean{FABL.booleanInfluence_majority_odd}
\label{FABL.booleanInfluence_majority_odd}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsBoundaryDimensionEdge, FABL.booleanInfluence, FABL.booleanInfluence_eq_dimensionEdgeBoundaryFraction, FABL.dimensionEdgeBoundaryFraction, FABL.dimensionEdgeRemoveEquiv, FABL.isBoundaryDimensionEdge_majority_odd_iff, FABL.majority, FABL.positiveCoordinateCount, FABL.uniformProbability, FABL.uniformProbability_positiveCoordinateCount_eq}
\difficulty{4}
For every nonnegative integer $m$ and every coordinate $i$ of the $(2m+1)$-dimensional
Boolean cube, the influence of coordinate $i$ for majority on that cube is
$$\\frac{\\binom{2m}{m}}{2^{2m}}.$$
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence of three-bit majority]
\lean{FABL.booleanInfluence_majority_three}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p046-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p062-b012
}
\label{FABL.booleanInfluence_majority_three}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.booleanInfluence, FABL.booleanInfluence_majority_odd, FABL.majority}
\difficulty{3}
For every coordinate $i$ of the three-dimensional Boolean cube, the influence of
coordinate $i$ for majority is $1/2$.
\end{theorem}
